01 / Meet the orchids

Small wonders. Remarkable adaptations.

Orchids belong to the flowering-plant family Orchidaceae. Their extraordinary variety of flowers, growth forms, and ecological relationships makes them an important group to study and conserve.

🌳

Epiphytic

Grow on tree trunks or branches for physical support. They are not automatically parasites of the tree.

🌱

Terrestrial

Grow on the ground, with roots in soil, leaf litter, or other suitable forest substrates.

🪨

Lithophytic

Some orchid species are adapted to grow on rocks and in rock crevices.

03 / Ecology

Orchids are part of a bigger story

Understanding orchids also means understanding the forests, trees, soil, fungi, and pollinators that help sustain them.

🌿

Forest microhabitats

Shade, moisture, airflow, and the structure of a tree or forest floor can shape the conditions in which an orchid grows.

🦋

Living relationships

Many orchids rely on specialised pollinators, and orchid seeds commonly depend on compatible fungi during germination.

💧

Adaptation & survival

Roots, leaves, and growth patterns reflect adaptations to different conditions. Requirements vary between species.

04 / Protect what makes us unique

Conservation begins with awareness.

Wild orchids are part of the natural heritage of forests and landscapes. Protecting habitats helps protect the many relationships that allow biodiversity to thrive.

⚠️ Challenges to watch

  • Deforestation and habitat loss
  • Changes in land use and infrastructure expansion
  • Illegal collection and overharvesting
  • Climate variability and changing local conditions

✓ What conservation can do

  • Monitor wild populations over time
  • Protect and restore natural habitats
  • Support responsible botanical research and conservation
  • Work with local communities to build awareness
Be an orchid guardian: Never remove wild orchids from their habitat. Avoid buying plants collected illegally from the wild, and share reliable information about native biodiversity.
